subject: ELA
title: ELA 5
description: Fifth-grade English Language Arts built around whole novels (Hatchet, Esperanza Rising, The Secret Garden), classic short stories, narrative and lyric poetry, Greek myths, and informational texts tied to early American history. Every week integrates close reading with text evidence, Greek and Latin word study, grammar and conventions, a writing product (narrative, informative/research or opinion), and a speaking and listening task. Students build a writing portfolio and finish the year with a multimedia research presentation.
framework: California Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts & Literacy; 2014 CA ELA/ELD Framework

standards.RL.5.1: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what it says explicitly and when drawing inferences.
standards.RL.5.2: Determine a theme from details, including how characters respond to challenges or a speaker reflects; summarize the text.
standards.RL.5.3: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events, drawing on specific details.
standards.RL.5.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as used in a text, including figurative language such as metaphors and similes.
standards.RL.5.5: Explain how chapters, scenes, or stanzas fit together to provide the overall structure of a story, drama, or poem.
standards.RL.5.6: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view influences how events are described.
standards.RL.5.7: Analyze how visual and multimedia elements contribute to the meaning, tone, or beauty of a text.
standards.RL.5.9: Compare and contrast stories in the same genre (e.g., mysteries, adventure, myths) on their approaches to similar themes and topics.
standards.RL.5.10: Read and comprehend grade 4–5 literature, including stories, dramas, and poetry, independently and proficiently.
standards.RI.5.1: Quote accurately from an informational text when explaining what it says explicitly and when drawing inferences.
standards.RI.5.2: Determine two or more main ideas of a text, explain how key details support them, and summarize the text.
standards.RI.5.3: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical or scientific text.
standards.RI.5.4: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a grade 5 text.
standards.RI.5.5: Compare and contrast the overall structure (chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of two or more texts.
standards.RI.5.6: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in point of view.
standards.RI.5.7: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources to locate an answer or solve a problem efficiently.
standards.RI.5.8: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points, identifying which reasons support which points.
standards.RI.5.9: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
standards.RI.5.10: Read and comprehend grade 4–5 informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, independently.
standards.RF.5.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills, using letter-sound correspondences, syllabication, and morphology (roots and affixes) to read unfamiliar multisyllabic words.
standards.RF.5.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension, including oral reading with appropriate rate and expression.
standards.W.5.1: Write opinion pieces that support a point of view with reasons and information, logically ordered and linked, with a concluding section.
standards.W.5.2: Write informative/explanatory texts that examine a topic and convey ideas clearly, using facts, definitions, details, quotations, and domain vocabulary.
standards.W.5.3: Write narratives using effective technique, descriptive details, dialogue, pacing, and clear event sequences.
standards.W.5.4: Produce clear and coherent writing in which development and organization are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
standards.W.5.5: Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.
standards.W.5.6: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing; type a minimum of two pages in a single sitting.
standards.W.5.7: Conduct short research projects that use several sources to build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.
standards.W.5.8: Recall or gather relevant information from experience and print/digital sources; summarize or paraphrase in notes and provide a list of sources.
standards.W.5.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
standards.W.5.10: Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.
standards.SL.5.1: Engage effectively in collaborative discussions, coming prepared, following agreed-upon rules, posing and responding to questions, and building on others' ideas.
standards.SL.5.2: Summarize a written text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats.
standards.SL.5.3: Summarize the points a speaker makes and explain how each claim is supported by reasons and evidence.
standards.SL.5.4: Report on a topic or text or present an opinion, sequencing ideas logically with appropriate facts and details; speak clearly at an understandable pace.
standards.SL.5.5: Include multimedia components and visual displays in presentations when appropriate to enhance main ideas or themes.
standards.SL.5.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, using formal English when appropriate.
standards.L.5.1a: Explain the function of conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections in general and in particular sentences.
standards.L.5.1b: Form and use the perfect verb tenses (I had walked; I have walked; I will have walked).
standards.L.5.1c: Use verb tense to convey various times, sequences, states, and conditions.
standards.L.5.1d: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in verb tense.
standards.L.5.2a: Use punctuation to separate items in a series.
standards.L.5.2b: Use a comma to separate an introductory element from the rest of the sentence.
standards.L.5.2c: Use a comma to set off yes and no, a tag question, and to indicate direct address.
standards.L.5.2d: Use underlining, quotation marks, or italics to indicate titles of works.
standards.L.5.2e: Spell grade-appropriate words correctly, consulting references as needed.
standards.L.5.3a: Expand, combine, and reduce sentences for meaning, reader/listener interest, and style.
standards.L.5.3b: Compare and contrast the varieties of English (dialects, registers) used in stories, dramas, or poems.
standards.L.5.4a: Use context (cause/effect, comparisons) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
standards.L.5.4b: Use common grade-appropriate Greek and Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word.
standards.L.5.4c: Consult reference materials (dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses) to find pronunciation and clarify precise meaning.
standards.L.5.5a: Interpret figurative language, including similes and metaphors, in context.
standards.L.5.5b: Recognize and explain the meaning of common idioms, adages, and proverbs.
standards.L.5.5c: Use the relationship between particular words (synonyms, antonyms, homographs) to better understand each word.
standards.L.5.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words, including those that signal contrast, addition, and logical relationships.

units.title: Launching: Short Stories and Personal Narrative
units.big_idea: Writers turn ordinary moments into stories by choosing vivid details and showing how a character changes.

units.title: Novel Study: Hatchet and the Survival Story
units.big_idea: Characters reveal who they are by how they respond to challenges.

units.title: Exploring Early America: Informational Reading and Research
units.big_idea: Readers compare multiple accounts and sources to build a fuller, fairer picture of the past.

units.title: Poetry: Sound, Image and Meaning
units.big_idea: Poets choose every word, sound and line break to create images and feeling.

units.title: Historical Fiction: Esperanza Rising
units.big_idea: Historical fiction helps us understand how real events shape ordinary people's lives.

units.title: Making a Case: Opinion Reading and Writing
units.big_idea: A strong opinion is supported by logically ordered reasons and evidence.

units.title: Classic Literature and Drama: The Secret Garden
units.big_idea: Settings and relationships can change characters, and drama brings story structure to life.

units.title: Myths and Comparing Genres
units.big_idea: Myths from many cultures explain the world and teach lessons about human nature.

units.title: Inquiry and Multimedia Presentation
units.big_idea: Researchers synthesize sources and use media to teach an audience.

weeks.topic: Reading 'Eleven' by Sandra Cisneros; writer's notebook launch
objectives: Quote accurately to explain a narrator's feelings
Generate personal narrative ideas in a writer's notebook
materials: 'Eleven' by Sandra Cisneros (in Woman Hollering Creek or online anthologies)

days.title: Narrator's voice
days.work: Read 'Eleven' aloud together and highlight every simile Rachel uses for being eleven; discuss what the comparisons reveal about her feelings.

days.title: Quoting evidence
days.work: Answer 4 inference questions about Rachel and Mrs. Price, quoting exact sentences with quotation marks; mini-lesson on conjunctions (and, but, because).

days.title: Writer's notebook
days.work: Set up a writer's notebook and create a 'heart map' and 'memory timeline' of 10 small moments that could become narratives.

days.title: Discussion and fluency
days.work: Hold a family book discussion on 'Is Rachel's reaction fair?' using sentence stems, then do a 1-minute fluency read of a passage and record words per minute.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph explaining how first-person point of view affects the story, with two quotations, and complete a conjunction identification quiz.

weeks.assessment: Evidence paragraph scored for accurate quoting; conjunction quiz; baseline fluency WPM.

weeks.topic: 'The Ransom of Red Chief' by O. Henry; character and plot
objectives: Summarize plot and compare characters
Plan a personal narrative with a clear sequence of events
materials: 'The Ransom of Red Chief' (Project Gutenberg, O. Henry 'Whirligigs')

days.title: Reading the story
days.work: Read 'The Ransom of Red Chief' (partner reading with an adult; the story contains dated language, which is discussed) and mark the moments where the plan backfires.

days.title: Word study: prefixes
days.work: Study prefixes un-, re-, dis-, mis-, pre- with 20 multisyllabic words, sorting and defining them; read 10 tricky words from the story by syllables.

days.title: Comparing characters
days.work: Use a Venn diagram to compare Bill and Sam with Red Chief, citing three details for each, and write a 5-sentence summary of the plot.

days.title: Narrative planning
days.work: Choose a small moment from the notebook and fill a story arc (beginning, rising action, climax, resolution); mini-lesson on prepositions and prepositional phrases.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a reading check on situational irony and plot sequence and a prefix quiz; share the story arc aloud.

weeks.assessment: Summary and Venn diagram; prefix quiz; narrative plan check-in.

weeks.topic: 'Thank You, Ma'am' by Langston Hughes; drafting narratives
objectives: Determine theme from how a character responds to a challenge
Draft a narrative using dialogue and description

days.title: Theme from actions
days.work: Read 'Thank You, Ma'am' and track what Mrs. Jones does and says at three points; write a theme statement supported by those actions.

days.title: Dialogue craft
days.work: Study how Hughes uses dialogue to show character; punctuate 10 lines of dialogue and learn interjections (Oh!, Well,).

days.title: Drafting the lead
days.work: Draft the opening of the personal narrative three ways (action, dialogue, sensory description) and choose the strongest.

days.title: Drafting the middle
days.work: Draft the rest of the narrative, including at least 4 lines of dialogue and commas in a series of sensory details.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Discuss theme with a partner using 'I think... because in the text...' stems, then take a quiz on dialogue punctuation and commas in a series.

weeks.assessment: Theme statement with evidence; complete narrative draft; punctuation quiz.

weeks.topic: 'All Summer in a Day' by Ray Bradbury; revising and publishing narratives
objectives: Analyze how setting shapes events
Revise and publish a personal narrative
materials: 'All Summer in a Day' (library anthology or CommonLit)

days.title: Setting and mood
days.work: Read 'All Summer in a Day' and list Bradbury's descriptions of rain and sun; explain how the Venus setting causes the conflict.

days.title: Revising for pacing
days.work: Revise the narrative by slowing down the most important moment with thoughts, feelings and sensory details (stretch it to at least a full paragraph).

days.title: Editing
days.work: Edit with a checklist for dialogue punctuation, commas in series, spelling and verb tense, then read it aloud to catch errors.

days.title: Publishing
days.work: Type the final narrative (aim for two pages in one sitting) and read it aloud to family as an author's chair.

days.title: Unit 1 assessment
days.work: Take a cold-read assessment on an unfamiliar short story (theme, character, quoting evidence) and a root/prefix vocabulary quiz.

weeks.assessment: Published personal narrative scored with a narrative rubric; Unit 1 cold-read assessment.

weeks.topic: Hatchet chapters 1–4: the crash
objectives: Analyze how the author builds suspense
Identify Brian's internal and external conflicts

days.title: Chapters 1–2
days.work: Read chapters 1–2 and list sentences Paulsen uses to create suspense (short fragments, repetition); explain the effect of one.

days.title: Flashbacks
days.work: Read chapter 3 and identify the flashback to 'the Secret'; explain how this chapter fits the overall structure of the opening.

days.title: Perfect tenses
days.work: Learn present, past and future perfect tenses with examples from Hatchet and write 9 sentences about the crash using each tense.

days.title: Chapter 4 and conflict
days.work: Read chapter 4 and create a two-column chart of Brian's internal and external conflicts with page numbers.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Discuss 'What would you do first?' using text evidence, then take a quiz on chapters 1–4 and perfect tenses.

weeks.assessment: Reading journal entries; chapters 1–4 quiz including perfect tense items.

weeks.topic: Hatchet chapters 5–9: first days of survival
objectives: Trace Brian's changing mindset
Interpret figurative language

days.title: Chapters 5–6
days.work: Read chapters 5–6 and mark three moments where Brian makes a decision; rate each as smart or risky with evidence.

days.title: Figurative language
days.work: Collect 6 similes, metaphors or personifications from chapters 5–7 and explain what each shows about Brian's situation.

days.title: Paired informational text
days.work: Read a ReadWorks wilderness survival article, identify two main ideas and compare its advice to Brian's choices.

days.title: Chapters 8–9
days.work: Read chapters 8–9 (the porcupine and fire) and write a journal entry on why the hatchet becomes so important.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on chapters 5–9 and figurative language, and practice verb tense to show sequence in 5 sentences.

weeks.assessment: Figurative language chart; journal entry using evidence; chapters 5–9 quiz.

weeks.topic: Hatchet chapters 10–13: the new Brian
objectives: Analyze character change over time
Use Greek and Latin roots to determine meaning

days.title: Chapters 10–11
days.work: Read chapters 10–11 and compare 'old Brian' and 'new Brian' on a T-chart with quotations.

days.title: Roots: spect, port, struct, rupt
days.work: Learn 4 Latin roots and build 16 words; find any of them in Hatchet and define them in context.

days.title: Chapters 12–13
days.work: Read chapters 12–13 (the plane passing, the low point) and discuss how this turning point changes Brian.

days.title: Narrative scene
days.work: Write a one-page scene from the point of view of an animal watching Brian, avoiding shifts in verb tense.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Correct 10 sentences with inappropriate tense shifts and take a roots quiz.

weeks.assessment: Character change T-chart; animal-POV scene; roots and tense-shift quiz.

weeks.topic: Hatchet chapters 14–17: the moose and the tornado
objectives: Explain how chapters build toward the climax
Determine theme from Brian's response to setbacks

days.title: Chapters 14–15
days.work: Read chapters 14–15 and plot the major events of the novel so far on a plot mountain.

days.title: Chapter 16
days.work: Read chapter 16 (the tornado) and list what Brian lost and what he still has, explaining his reaction.

days.title: Chapter 17
days.work: Read chapter 17 and discuss the theme of resilience in a Socratic-style conversation, citing two page numbers.

days.title: Fluency and expression
days.work: Practice reading a dramatic passage from chapter 16 three times with expression and record the final reading.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a theme paragraph: 'What does Hatchet teach about mistakes?' with two quotations and explanation.

weeks.assessment: Theme paragraph scored on claim, evidence and explanation; fluency recording.

weeks.topic: Hatchet chapters 18–19 and epilogue; literary essay
objectives: Analyze how the epilogue affects meaning
Write a literary response essay using evidence

days.title: Finishing the novel
days.work: Read chapters 18–19 and the epilogue; discuss how the epilogue changes our view of Brian's experience.

days.title: Essay planning
days.work: Choose a prompt (How does Brian change?) and fill an organizer with a thesis, three reasons and quotations.

days.title: Drafting
days.work: Draft a five-paragraph literary essay with an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion.

days.title: Revising and editing
days.work: Revise for transition words and evidence explanation; edit for perfect-tense verbs and spelling.

days.title: Unit 2 assessment
days.work: Take the Unit 2 assessment on Hatchet (character, theme, figurative language, roots) and submit the final essay.

weeks.assessment: Literary essay rubric; Unit 2 test.

weeks.topic: Informational text structures: navigating the oceans
objectives: Identify text structures in informational articles
Determine meanings of domain-specific words
materials: ReadWorks articles on exploration and navigation

days.title: Text structure overview
days.work: Learn five text structures and their signal words, then sort 10 short paragraphs about exploration by structure.

days.title: Comparing structures
days.work: Read two articles on navigation tools (one chronological, one problem/solution) and compare their structures in a chart.

days.title: Domain vocabulary
days.work: Use context and a dictionary to define 10 navigation terms (compass, sextant, latitude) and draw a labeled picture of two.

days.title: Main ideas
days.work: Identify two main ideas in an article about the Age of Exploration and summarize it in 5 sentences.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a text structure quiz and a domain vocabulary check.

weeks.assessment: Text structure quiz; vocabulary check; written summary.

weeks.topic: Multiple accounts: Columbus and the Taíno
objectives: Analyze similarities and differences in point of view across accounts
Quote accurately from primary and secondary sources
materials: excerpt of Columbus's 1492 journal (Library of Congress / National Archives sites)
Smithsonian NMAI article on the Taíno

days.title: Primary source
days.work: Read an excerpt of Columbus's journal from October 1492 and note how he describes the land and the Taíno people.

days.title: Another perspective
days.work: Read a secondary source about Taíno life and the effects of contact, noting the author's point of view.

days.title: Comparing accounts
days.work: Complete a chart comparing what each account emphasizes and leaves out, quoting both.

days.title: Discussion
days.work: Discuss 'Why do accounts of the same event differ?' and learn Greek roots graph, tele, geo, chron.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph analyzing two points of view with quotations, and take a Greek roots quiz.

weeks.assessment: Point-of-view comparison paragraph; Greek roots quiz.

weeks.topic: Biography: 'And Then What Happened, Paul Revere?' by Jean Fritz; research launch
objectives: Explain relationships between individuals and events
Choose a research topic and generate questions
materials: 'And Then What Happened, Paul Revere?' by Jean Fritz (library)

days.title: Reading the biography
days.work: Read the Jean Fritz biography and make a timeline of Paul Revere's life events.

days.title: Relationships
days.work: Explain how three events or people (Sons of Liberty, the British, Revere's trade) influenced Revere's actions in a cause/effect chart.

days.title: Choosing a topic
days.work: Choose a research topic about colonial life or an explorer and write 4 research questions about different aspects of it.

days.title: Finding sources
days.work: Locate 3 sources (library book, encyclopedia, reliable website) and record them in a source list with titles italicized or underlined.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on the biography and on title punctuation, and conference with a parent on research questions.

weeks.assessment: Cause/effect chart; research questions and source list; title punctuation quiz.

weeks.topic: Research: note-taking and drafting an informative report
objectives: Paraphrase information in notes
Integrate information from several texts in an informative draft

days.title: Note-taking
days.work: Take 15 paraphrased note cards from 3 sources, coding each card to a research question and its source.

days.title: Paraphrase vs. plagiarism
days.work: Practice paraphrasing 5 passages and compare to the originals; finish note cards.

days.title: Outlining
days.work: Sort note cards into 3–4 subtopics and build an outline with headings.

days.title: Drafting
days.work: Draft the introduction and two body sections of the report using transition words like 'in addition' and 'however'.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Finish the draft with a conclusion and a list of sources; self-check against the informative rubric.

weeks.assessment: Note cards and outline; complete informative draft.

weeks.topic: Publishing and presenting the research report
objectives: Revise and type a research report
Present findings with a visual display

days.title: Revising
days.work: Revise the report for precise domain vocabulary and add one quotation and one text feature (map, diagram, timeline).

days.title: Typing and editing
days.work: Type the final report in one sitting and edit for commas, titles and spelling.

days.title: Visual display
days.work: Create a poster or 4-slide display highlighting the report's main ideas with captioned images.

days.title: Presenting
days.work: Present the report in 3–4 minutes to family, speaking clearly and answering two audience questions.

days.title: Unit 3 assessment
days.work: Take a cold-read assessment comparing two informational texts on the same topic (structure, point of view, integration).

weeks.assessment: Research report rubric; presentation checklist; Unit 3 assessment.

weeks.topic: Narrative poetry: 'Paul Revere's Ride' by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
objectives: Explain how stanzas build a narrative poem
Read poetry aloud with rhythm and expression

days.title: First read
days.work: Read 'Paul Revere's Ride' aloud and summarize what happens in each stanza in one line.

days.title: Structure and rhythm
days.work: Mark the rhyme scheme and galloping rhythm of the first three stanzas and explain how the sound matches the action.

days.title: Poem vs. history
days.work: Compare the poem's events with the Jean Fritz biography and list what Longfellow changed and why.

days.title: Imagery
days.work: Illustrate the three most vivid images from the poem and label the words that created each picture.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Recite two memorized stanzas with expression and take a quiz on stanza, rhyme scheme and imagery.

weeks.assessment: Recitation; poetry terms quiz; poem vs. history chart.

weeks.topic: Lyric poetry: Frost and Dickinson
objectives: Determine theme in poetry
Interpret metaphors and the speaker's point of view
materials: 'The Road Not Taken' and 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening' by Robert Frost
'Hope is the thing with feathers' by Emily Dickinson

days.title: 'The Road Not Taken'
days.work: Read the poem twice and discuss what the two roads symbolize; write the theme in one sentence.

days.title: 'Stopping by Woods'
days.work: Analyze the speaker's point of view and why the last line repeats; mark the rhyme scheme.

days.title: Dickinson's metaphor
days.work: Read 'Hope is the thing with feathers' and chart how hope is compared to a bird in each stanza.

days.title: Idioms and proverbs
days.work: Learn 12 common idioms, adages and proverbs ('cross that bridge when you come to it') and connect two to the poems.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write an extended-metaphor poem of your own (e.g., 'Courage is...') and take an idioms quiz.

weeks.assessment: Original metaphor poem; idioms/proverbs quiz; theme sentences.

weeks.topic: Poets play with language: Hughes and Carroll; poetry anthology
objectives: Compare varieties of English and invented language in poems
Compile and perform an original poetry anthology
materials: 'Dreams' and 'April Rain Song' by Langston Hughes

days.title: Langston Hughes
days.work: Read 'Dreams' and 'April Rain Song', identify the metaphor and personification, and write a free-verse weather poem.

days.title: 'Jabberwocky'
days.work: Read 'Jabberwocky' and use grammar clues to decide the part of speech and meaning of 8 nonsense words.

days.title: Varieties of English
days.work: Compare formal and informal registers in poems and rewrite a stanza in a different register.

days.title: Anthology
days.work: Compile 5 original poems (narrative stanza, metaphor, free verse, rhyme, nonsense) into an illustrated anthology.

days.title: Unit 4 assessment
days.work: Hold a poetry café reading of 2 original poems and take a cold-read poetry assessment on theme and figurative language.

weeks.assessment: Poetry anthology rubric; performance; Unit 4 cold-read assessment.

weeks.topic: Esperanza Rising: 'Aguascalientes, Mexico 1924' – Las Uvas through Las Guayabas
objectives: Analyze the setting and its historical context
Describe Esperanza's character at the start
materials: Esperanza Rising by Pam Muñoz Ryan (library)

days.title: Las Uvas
days.work: Read 'Las Uvas' and describe the setting of El Rancho de las Rosas with 5 details; locate Aguascalientes on a map.

days.title: Las Papayas
days.work: Read 'Las Papayas' and discuss how Papa's death changes everything; mark Spanish words and use context to define them.

days.title: Point of view
days.work: Explain how the third-person limited narrator shows events through Esperanza's eyes, using 2 quotations.

days.title: Los Higos and Las Guayabas
days.work: Read 'Los Higos' and 'Las Guayabas' and create a character trait web for Esperanza with evidence.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on the first four chapters and write a journal entry as Esperanza leaving Mexico.

weeks.assessment: Character trait web; journal entry; chapter quiz.

weeks.topic: Esperanza Rising: arrival in California – Los Melones through Las Almendras
objectives: Compare Esperanza's life in Mexico and California
Use correlative conjunctions

days.title: Los Melones
days.work: Read 'Los Melones' (the train journey) and discuss how Esperanza treats Isabel and the peasant girl.

days.title: Las Cebollas
days.work: Read 'Las Cebollas' and compare Esperanza's old and new homes in a Venn diagram.

days.title: Correlative conjunctions
days.work: Learn either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also and write 8 sentences about the novel using them.

days.title: Las Almendras
days.work: Read 'Las Almendras' and write a paragraph on what Esperanza learns from sweeping the platform.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Discuss in a book talk how Esperanza is changing, then take a quiz on chapters and correlative conjunctions.

weeks.assessment: Venn diagram; paragraph with evidence; grammar quiz.

weeks.topic: Esperanza Rising: Las Ciruelas, Las Papas, Los Aguacates
objectives: Analyze conflict between characters' viewpoints on the strike
Distinguish synonyms, antonyms and homographs
materials: ReadWorks or CommonLit article on the Great Depression and farmworkers

days.title: Las Ciruelas
days.work: Read 'Las Ciruelas' and list the arguments of Marta and Miguel about the strike.

days.title: Las Papas
days.work: Read 'Las Papas' and explain how Mama's illness changes Esperanza's responsibilities.

days.title: Informational connection
days.work: Read an informational article on 1930s farmworkers and Mexican repatriation and note 3 facts the novel reflects.

days.title: Los Aguacates
days.work: Read 'Los Aguacates' and practice synonyms, antonyms and homographs (wind/wind, lead/lead) with 15 words.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a 'Two Sides' paragraph on whether Miguel or Marta has the better plan and take a word relationships quiz.

weeks.assessment: Two-sides paragraph; informational notes; word relationships quiz.

weeks.topic: Esperanza Rising: Los Espárragos, Los Duraznos, Las Uvas
objectives: Determine the novel's theme
Explain how chapter titles structure the novel

days.title: Los Espárragos
days.work: Read 'Los Espárragos' and discuss the betrayal and Esperanza's decision about Abuelita's money.

days.title: Los Duraznos
days.work: Read 'Los Duraznos' and track the symbol of the phoenix and the blanket through the book.

days.title: Las Uvas
days.work: Read the final chapter and explain why the novel ends with the same fruit it begins with.

days.title: Theme
days.work: Write 2 theme statements and support each with 3 pieces of evidence from across the novel.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a whole-novel reading assessment on plot, character change and symbolism.

weeks.assessment: Theme organizer; novel assessment.

weeks.topic: Comparing stories: Esperanza Rising and Hatchet; compare-contrast essay
objectives: Compare how two novels approach a similar theme
Write a compare-contrast informative essay

days.title: Planning the comparison
days.work: Use an organizer to compare how Brian and Esperanza face loss and change, with 2 quotations from each book.

days.title: Drafting
days.work: Draft a compare-contrast essay using point-by-point or block structure and contrast transitions.

days.title: Dialect and language
days.work: Compare the use of Spanish words and dialect in Esperanza Rising with Paulsen's plain style and add a paragraph on language.

days.title: Revising and editing
days.work: Revise with a peer/parent checklist, edit, and type the final essay.

days.title: Unit 5 assessment
days.work: Discuss the two novels in a book talk and take a cold-read assessment comparing two short stories with similar themes.

weeks.assessment: Compare-contrast essay rubric; Unit 5 cold-read assessment.

weeks.topic: Analyzing arguments: reasons and evidence
objectives: Identify an author's points and supporting reasons and evidence
Summarize a speaker's claims
materials: paired opinion articles from CommonLit or ReadWorks (e.g., on homework or zoos)

days.title: What is an argument?
days.work: Read a short opinion article and map its claim, reasons and evidence on a graphic organizer.

days.title: Evaluating evidence
days.work: Rate 10 pieces of evidence as fact, statistic, expert quote or opinion and decide which are strongest.

days.title: Two sides
days.work: Read paired articles on whether zoos help animals and compare which reasons each author uses.

days.title: Listening for claims
days.work: Watch a short student speech or news segment and summarize the speaker's claims and supporting reasons.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz identifying claims and matching reasons to points in a new article.

weeks.assessment: Argument maps; reasons-and-evidence quiz.

weeks.topic: Planning an opinion essay
objectives: Choose an opinion and gather reasons from multiple sources
Organize reasons logically

days.title: Choosing a position
days.work: Choose a debatable question (e.g., Should schools have longer recess?) and write a clear opinion statement.

days.title: Gathering evidence
days.work: Gather 6 facts or quotes from at least 2 sources and record them with source names.

days.title: Organizing reasons
days.work: Group evidence under 3 reasons and order them from least to most convincing.

days.title: Introductory elements
days.work: Learn commas after introductory words, phrases and clauses and write 10 sentences for the essay using them.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Conference on the organizer and take a quiz on commas with introductory elements.

weeks.assessment: Completed opinion organizer; comma quiz.

weeks.topic: Drafting and revising the opinion essay
objectives: Draft an opinion essay with linking words
Revise for clear reasoning and a strong conclusion

days.title: Introduction
days.work: Draft an introduction with a hook, background and opinion statement.

days.title: Body paragraphs
days.work: Draft three body paragraphs linking reasons and evidence with words like 'consequently' and 'specifically'.

days.title: Counterclaim and conclusion
days.work: Add a sentence addressing the other side and draft a conclusion that restates the opinion and calls readers to act.

days.title: Commas for yes/no, tags and address
days.work: Learn commas for yes/no, tag questions and direct address and edit dialogue examples, then revise the essay with a checklist.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Read the draft aloud to a family member who gives two 'glows' and one 'grow', and revise accordingly.

weeks.assessment: Complete revised draft; comma quiz embedded in editing.

weeks.topic: Publishing and debating
objectives: Publish a typed opinion essay
Present an opinion orally and respond to counterarguments

days.title: Final copy
days.work: Type and format the final opinion essay with a title and source list.

days.title: Debate prep
days.work: Turn the essay into a 2-minute opening statement on note cards and prepare rebuttals to 2 likely counterarguments.

days.title: Debate
days.work: Debate the question with a family member or co-op partner using formal English and timed turns.

days.title: Reflection
days.work: Summarize the opponent's best reasons and write whether they changed your thinking.

days.title: Unit 6 assessment
days.work: Take a cold-read assessment analyzing reasons and evidence and write an on-demand opinion paragraph in 30 minutes.

weeks.assessment: Opinion essay rubric; debate observation; Unit 6 on-demand writing.

weeks.topic: The Secret Garden chapters 1–7: Mary arrives at Misselthwaite
objectives: Describe how the setting reflects Mary's character
Compare dialects in the novel
materials: The Secret Garden by Frances Hodgson Burnett (Project Gutenberg or library)

days.title: Chapters 1–2
days.work: Read chapters 1–2 and list 5 details showing Mary is 'contrary'; discuss why she behaves that way.

days.title: Chapters 3–4
days.work: Read chapters 3–4 and describe Misselthwaite Manor and the moor; draw the setting with labels.

days.title: Yorkshire dialect
days.work: Translate 8 lines of Martha's Yorkshire dialect into standard English and discuss why Burnett includes dialect.

days.title: Chapters 5–7
days.work: Read chapters 5–7 (the cry in the corridor, the robin, finding the key) and predict what the key opens.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on chapters 1–7 and read a dialect passage aloud for fluency.

weeks.assessment: Setting drawing; dialect translation; chapter quiz.

weeks.topic: The Secret Garden chapters 8–15: the garden and Dickon
objectives: Analyze how relationships change Mary
Combine and expand sentences for style

days.title: Chapters 8–10
days.work: Read chapters 8–10 and compare the garden's condition to Mary's condition at the start.

days.title: Chapters 11–12
days.work: Read chapters 11–12 and write a character sketch of Dickon with 3 quotations.

days.title: Sentence combining
days.work: Combine, expand and reduce 12 sentences from the novel to improve style.

days.title: Chapters 13–15
days.work: Read chapters 13–15 and compare Mary and Colin as two 'contrary' children in a chart.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a descriptive paragraph of the garden in spring using combined sentences and sensory details.

weeks.assessment: Character sketch; descriptive paragraph; comparison chart.

weeks.topic: The Secret Garden chapters 16–22: Colin's change
objectives: Trace the theme of healing
Analyze illustrations and film elements
materials: an illustrated edition or the 1949 or 1993 film adaptation

days.title: Chapters 16–18
days.work: Read chapters 16–18 and track Colin's attitude in a 'before and after' chart.

days.title: Chapters 19–20
days.work: Read chapters 19–20 and explain what the children mean by 'Magic.'

days.title: Visual elements
days.work: Compare an illustrated edition's pictures (or a film scene) with the text and explain how they add to mood.

days.title: Chapters 21–22
days.work: Read chapters 21–22 and discuss how Colin's standing up is a turning point.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a theme paragraph about healing in nature with evidence from three chapters.

weeks.assessment: Theme paragraph; visual analysis notes.

weeks.topic: The Secret Garden chapters 23–27 and readers' theater
objectives: Explain how scenes structure a drama
Perform a readers' theater adaptation

days.title: Finishing the novel
days.work: Read chapters 23–27 and summarize how the ending resolves Mary's, Colin's and Mr. Craven's stories.

days.title: Story vs. drama
days.work: Study a sample script's scenes, cast list and stage directions, and compare its structure to chapters.

days.title: Writing a script
days.work: Adapt one key chapter (finding the garden or Colin's first visit) into a 2-scene readers' theater script.

days.title: Rehearsal
days.work: Rehearse the script with family members, focusing on expression, pacing and dialect.

days.title: Unit 7 assessment
days.work: Perform the readers' theater and take an assessment on the novel's structure, characters and theme.

weeks.assessment: Script and performance rubric; Unit 7 novel assessment.

weeks.topic: Greek myths: gods, heroes and lessons
objectives: Determine the lesson of a myth
Use Greek roots and myth-based words
materials: A Wonder-Book by Nathaniel Hawthorne (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: The Olympians
days.work: Read the D'Aulaires' chapters on Zeus and the Olympians and make a family tree with each god's domain.

days.title: 'The Golden Touch'
days.work: Read Hawthorne's 'The Golden Touch' (King Midas) and write the lesson in one sentence with evidence.

days.title: 'The Paradise of Children'
days.work: Read Hawthorne's Pandora story and compare how it explains troubles in the world.

days.title: Words from myths
days.work: Learn 12 words and phrases from mythology (Midas touch, panic, echo, Herculean) and explain their origins.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Summarize a myth aloud in 1 minute and take a quiz on myth vocabulary and lessons.

weeks.assessment: Myth lesson statements; allusion vocabulary quiz; oral summary.

weeks.topic: Myths across cultures: comparing themes
objectives: Compare myths from different cultures on similar themes
Explain adages and proverbs from folklore
materials: Native American and West African trickster or origin tales (library collections or CommonLit)

days.title: Prometheus
days.work: Read the myth of Prometheus bringing fire and note what it explains and the hero's traits.

days.title: Another culture's fire story
days.work: Read a Native American fire-bringing tale (e.g., Grandmother Spider or Coyote) and note what it explains.

days.title: Trickster tales
days.work: Read an Anansi tale and compare the trickster to Coyote and Prometheus in a matrix.

days.title: Writing the comparison
days.work: Write two paragraphs comparing how two myths approach the theme of sharing knowledge or fire.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a cold-read quiz comparing two new folktales on theme.

weeks.assessment: Comparison paragraphs; cold-read quiz.

weeks.topic: Writing an original myth
objectives: Write a myth that explains a natural phenomenon
Use narrative techniques including pacing and dialogue

days.title: Planning
days.work: Choose a phenomenon (why the moon changes shape, why cats purr) and plan a myth with characters, conflict and explanation.

days.title: Drafting
days.work: Draft the myth with dialogue and a god, hero or trickster character.

days.title: Revising
days.work: Revise for pacing (summarize travel, slow down the key scene) and vivid verbs.

days.title: Publishing
days.work: Type and illustrate the myth as a small book.

days.title: Unit 8 assessment
days.work: Read the myth aloud to an audience and take a Greek/Latin roots cumulative quiz.

weeks.assessment: Original myth narrative rubric; roots cumulative quiz.

weeks.topic: Inquiry: researching a California national park or natural wonder
objectives: Locate information efficiently in multiple sources
Take notes and list sources

days.title: Choosing and questioning
days.work: Choose a CA national park (Yosemite, Joshua Tree, Redwood, Death Valley) and write 5 inquiry questions.

days.title: Searching efficiently
days.work: Practice keyword searching and evaluating credibility of 4 websites, then find answers on nps.gov.

days.title: Note-taking
days.work: Take paraphrased notes from 3 sources organized by question.

days.title: Synthesis
days.work: Write a synthesis paragraph combining information from at least 2 sources on one question.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Conference on notes and source list; complete a source credibility checklist.

weeks.assessment: Notes and source list; synthesis paragraph.

weeks.topic: Building a multimedia presentation
objectives: Write informative slide text and a script
Integrate images, maps or audio to enhance main ideas

days.title: Storyboarding
days.work: Storyboard 8 slides: title, 5 content slides, conclusion and sources.

days.title: Writing slide text
days.work: Write concise slide text and a full speaker script for each slide.

days.title: Adding media
days.work: Add a map, captioned photos and one audio or video element that supports a main idea, crediting sources.

days.title: Editing
days.work: Edit script and slides for spelling and conventions, and practice timing to 5 minutes.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Do a full rehearsal for a family member and revise based on feedback.

weeks.assessment: Storyboard, script and slide deck checklist.

weeks.topic: Presentation and year-end portfolio
objectives: Deliver a multimedia presentation
Reflect on growth as a reader and writer

days.title: Presentation day
days.work: Deliver the multimedia presentation and answer audience questions.

days.title: Listening and summarizing
days.work: Watch a family member's or online presentation and summarize its main points and supporting details.

days.title: Portfolio selection
days.work: Choose the best narrative, informative and opinion pieces from the year and write a reflection card for each.

days.title: Reading reflection
days.work: List all books read this year, rate them, and write a letter to next year's self about reading goals; do a final fluency check.

days.title: End-of-year assessment
days.work: Take an end-of-year reading and writing assessment (cold read with evidence questions and an on-demand essay).

weeks.assessment: Presentation rubric; portfolio reflections; end-of-year assessment and fluency WPM compared to week 1.
